investigate:diagnostics.summary: I built per-mode training trajectories for G (runs/ppo-modes-seed0, game_modes block) and each specialist S from the train records, in 10 windows of 16 records (524,288 env steps per mode each), plus the eval curves and the 16-minibatch specialist controls. Four things stand out for constrictor. (1) G's value-loss weight there is about 0.30, against 1.0 for S and 1.1-1.5 for G's other modes. (2) G's explained variance stalls near 0.21 from about 2.5M steps, while S's keeps climbing to 0.35; about 60-75% of that gap comes from G's constrictor returns having less variance, not from a larger value error. (3) G learns constrictor survival slower than S early: it has about 0.24 more self-collision deaths per game until about 2.6M steps and catches up by about 4M. (4) Against heuristics, G's constrictor eval is flat from the first eval point at 1.05M (slope +0.008 +/- 0.014 per 1M steps, versus +0.025 to +0.065 for G's other modes), and G ends level with S (-0.005 +/- 0.029 pooled over the 5 evals). KL and clip fraction are not distinctive early; there is a weak, borderline-significant late reduction. Royale looks like the opposite case: G has much higher explained variance than S (+0.118), fewer self-collisions (-0.21 per game), more head-to-head deaths and a steeper eval curve. Most of G's lower entropy in standard and royale is the 16-minibatch setting, not multi-mode training (the 16-minibatch specialist matches it). Everything is one seed per run. Duel specialists across 3 seeds show optimizer diagnostics reproduce tightly but outcome stats such as draw rate do not (0.02-0.45), so I only trust the former at one-seed resolution.

findings.claim: Q1 (value-loss weight): constrictor gets by far the smallest value-loss weight in G, about 0.30 against 1.0 for any specialist. It is constant over training and takes only 7-8% of the total weight.
findings.evidence: G value_weight by 0.52M window (constrictor): 0.341, 0.306, 0.308, 0.311, 0.319, 0.319, 0.307, 0.301, 0.303, 0.298 (last window CI [0.292,0.303]). Standard is 1.50-1.55 (1.532 last), duel 0.96-1.08, royale 1.09-1.19 (1.094 last). Share of the total weight (w/4) in the last window: constrictor 0.074, standard 0.383, duel 0.269, royale 0.273. The weights track 1/return_var as designed: the formula from logged return_var matches the logged weight to ratio 0.997-1.003, with differences from chunk averaging. Constrictor return_var is 0.165-0.176 against 0.032-0.046 elsewhere. The 4-5x ratio probably reflects horizon and discounting (games of about 32 turns versus 170-250 turns at gamma 0.99), which is my inference rather than something I tested.

findings.claim: Q1 (value gradient size): the weighting equalises the squared weighted value loss across modes but not the gradient. Constrictor's value signal into the shared torso is about half that of the other modes, and about 3.3x smaller relative to its own policy gradient than a specialist's. This is a derived proxy, not a causal result.
findings.evidence: Weighted value loss w*v_loss, last window: standard 0.0189, duel 0.0205, royale 0.0176, constrictor 0.0191. Gradient proxy w*sqrt(2*v_loss): constrictor 0.107 (0.136 in the first window) against 0.241 standard, 0.210 duel, 0.196 royale. Effective value-to-policy weight is 0.3 versus S's 1.0 in constrictor, but 1.5x S's in standard. There is no value_norm-off or equal-weight run, so whether the weight matters is unknown. Weight does not order explained-variance gaps monotonically: royale (weight 1.1) is +0.118 and duel (weight 1.1) is -0.058.

findings.claim: Q1/Q2 (explained variance): G's constrictor explained variance stalls from about 2.4-2.6M env steps at about 0.20-0.22, while S's keeps rising to about 0.35. Constrictor is the only mode where G's training EV is badly below S's and flat while its other modes keep rising.
findings.evidence: EV by window, G constrictor: 0.084, 0.132, 0.162, 0.184, 0.203, 0.201, 0.224, 0.218, 0.221, 0.217. S: 0.132, 0.201, 0.232, 0.251, 0.268, 0.319, 0.338, 0.341, 0.372, 0.353. G-S last window -0.137 [-0.174,-0.105]; second half -0.128 [-0.147,-0.112] (block bootstrap, blocks of 4 records). EV slope over 2.1-5.24M per 1M steps: G constrictor +0.006 [-0.001,+0.014], S constrictor +0.033 [+0.015,+0.054], G standard +0.016, G royale +0.018, G duel +0.006. Last-window G-S in other modes: standard +0.109 [+0.096,+0.121], royale +0.118 [+0.107,+0.131], duel -0.058 [-0.072,-0.045]. Seed spread of EV across 3 duel specialists is 0.178-0.222, so these gaps are several times seed noise.

findings.claim: The constrictor EV deficit is mostly a lower-return-variance effect, not a much larger value error. This weakens 'G's value function is broken in constrictor'.
findings.evidence: v_loss = 0.5*MSE and EV = 1 - MSE/return_var reproduces the logged EV (G: 1-0.129/0.165 = 0.218, logged 0.217; S: 1-0.122/0.190 = 0.358, logged 0.353). Last window: G v_loss 0.064 versus S 0.061 (+0.004 [+0.002,+0.006], about +6% MSE) but return_var 0.165 versus 0.190 (-0.025 [-0.032,-0.019]). With S's variance and G's MSE, G's EV would be about 0.32, which closes about 76% of the gap (about 60% using the second-half averages). Standard and royale G have return_var 0.006-0.007 above S (0.032 vs 0.026; 0.045 vs 0.038), so the variance effect runs the other way there. Why G's constrictor returns are less variable I did not resolve.

findings.claim: Q2 (eval curve): G's constrictor eval against heuristics is flat from the first eval point, and the other G modes all improve significantly. There is no significant regression, only two low points that I picked after looking.
findings.evidence: Score (parity 0.25, 256 games, logged normal-approx 95% half-widths about 0.045) at 1.05/2.10/3.15/4.19/5.24M: G 0.204, 0.158, 0.158, 0.230, 0.208; S 0.111, 0.195, 0.230, 0.230, 0.234. Weighted-LS slope per 1M steps (SE = ci95/1.96): G constrictor +0.008 +/- 0.014 (chi2 vs constant 7.9, 4 dof, p=0.095); S constrictor +0.030 +/- 0.013; G standard +0.025 +/- 0.008; G duel +0.065 +/- 0.014; G royale +0.040 +/- 0.016. Pooled 5-point mean: G 0.188 +/- 0.020, S 0.186 +/- 0.020. 5.24M minus 1.05M for G: +0.005 +/- 0.066. The 2.10 and 3.15M points pooled (0.158 +/- 0.030) versus the other three (0.214 +/- 0.028) differ by -0.056 +/- 0.041, borderline and post hoc. G-S against heuristics in constrictor: +0.093 +/- 0.059 at 1.05M, then -0.037, -0.073, 0.000, -0.025; pooled over the last 3 evals -0.034 +/- 0.039, over all 5 -0.005 +/- 0.029. Against random_legal: G 0.680, 0.671, 0.727, 0.736, 0.714; S 0.673, 0.718, 0.755, 0.705, 0.672 (flat for both).

findings.claim: Q2 (self-play behaviour): G learns constrictor survival more slowly than S early and does not stall in self-play. By about 4M its self-play profile matches S's, so the head-to-head deficit is not visible in these self-play statistics.
findings.evidence: Self-collision deaths per game, G-S by 0.52M window: +0.24 [+0.17,+0.32], +0.24 [+0.18,+0.31], +0.19, +0.22, +0.26 [+0.21,+0.31], +0.11, +0.07, -0.03, -0.03, -0.06 [-0.10,-0.02] (block bootstrap). G's self-deaths fall from 1.57 to 1.12 (slope -0.104 per 1M steps [-0.125,-0.073] over 2.1-5.24M); S stays at 1.18-1.33 (slope +0.010 [-0.013,+0.046]). Mean game length G-S is about -2.1 turns from 0.5M to 2.6M (e.g. -2.2 [-2.4,-2.0]) and -0.0 [-0.7,+0.7] in the last window (32.5 vs 32.6). Head-to-head deaths G-S are -0.31 early and +0.03 [-0.06,+0.12] at the end. Draws per game are lower for G: 0.113 vs 0.140 (-0.027 [-0.032,-0.021]). G has 40,960 total gradient updates against S's 20,480, yet learned this more slowly. The G-S deficit in the 1024-game head-to-head (0.406) cannot be seen in these self-play stats; I infer it is a cross-play mismatch, which I did not test.

findings.claim: Q1 (KL, clip fraction, entropy) are not distinctive early. There is a weak, borderline late reduction in KL, and G's entropy in constrictor does not drop below S's, unlike in standard and royale.
findings.evidence: G/S approx_kl ratio, first half (records 0:80): standard 1.13 [1.05,1.22], duel 1.07 [0.98,1.16], royale 1.30 [1.22,1.39], constrictor 1.07 [1.00,1.15]. Second half (80:160): 1.07, 0.99, 1.14, constrictor 0.75 [0.54,1.04]. Last third (107:160): constrictor KL 0.67 [0.45,1.00], clip_frac 0.78 [0.54,1.11]; last-window clip_frac G 0.008 vs S 0.014 (-0.005 [-0.013,+0.002]). Entropy G/S last window: constrictor 0.148/0.131 (+0.017 [+0.010,+0.025]); standard 0.244/0.360; royale 0.238/0.337; duel 0.241/0.249. G's constrictor entropy slope is -0.040 per 1M steps against S's -0.044, so G is still sharpening. Mean top-level grad_norm stays below the 0.5 clip in all runs (G 0.21-0.31, S 0.23-0.46), but the log has only the mean, so per-step clipping is not ruled out.

findings.claim: The 16-minibatch control shows most of G's lower entropy in standard and royale comes from the minibatch count, not multi-mode training. G's explained-variance lead and its fewer self-collisions in royale are not explained by minibatches. G's per-mode KL per gradient step is about half a 16-minibatch specialist's.
findings.evidence: Records 80:144 (2.65-4.72M). Standard entropy: G 0.310, S8 0.404, S16 0.311. Royale entropy: G 0.300, S8 0.397, S16 0.318. EV: standard G 0.212, S8 0.097, S16 0.122; royale G 0.265, S8 0.137, S16 0.142. Royale self-deaths: G 0.493, S8 0.765, S16 0.816. Royale head-to-head deaths: G 1.140, S8 0.810, S16 0.855. Standard self-deaths: G 0.971, S8 1.190, S16 1.100; standard head-to-head: G 1.418, S8 0.904, S16 1.109, so minibatches explain only part there. approx_kl: standard G 0.005, S8 0.005, S16 0.011; royale G 0.005, S8 0.004, S16 0.011. No constrictor 16-minibatch specialist exists. If the standard and royale pattern held (S16 entropy about 0.09 below S8), a constrictor S16 would sit near 0.09 against G's 0.198 over the second half. That is an extrapolation, not a measurement. royale-m16 is incomplete (155 of 160 records), so I used only records up to 144.

findings.claim: Q3 (royale): G is clearly different from S in royale on every learning-curve diagnostic, and also stronger against heuristics.
findings.evidence: Last window G/S: EV 0.281/0.163 (+0.118 [+0.107,+0.131]); self-deaths 0.514/0.723 (-0.209 [-0.230,-0.181]); body deaths 0.265/0.428; head-to-head 1.059/0.731 (+0.328 [+0.269,+0.379]); hazard 0.830/0.756 (+0.074 [+0.026,+0.119]); starve 0.291/0.308 (no difference); game length 169/176 turns; draws 0.005/0.008; return_var 0.045/0.038; value_weight 1.094. G's royale self-collision gap is already -0.31 [-0.35,-0.25] in the 0.52-1.05M window, versus constrictor's +0.24 in the same window. Evals vs heuristics (parity 0.25), G 0.170, 0.217, 0.279, 0.307, 0.330 and S 0.104, 0.164, 0.146, 0.168, 0.203; G-S pooled over the last 3 evals +0.133 +/- 0.042. Slopes per 1M steps: G +0.040 +/- 0.016, S +0.020 +/- 0.013. Standard shows the same direction: EV 0.227 vs 0.117, self-deaths 1.07 vs 1.24, head-to-head 1.31 vs 0.88, G-S vs heuristics +0.082 +/- 0.023 (last 3).

findings.claim: Q4 (surprise, duel): the duel specialist drifts into a draw-heavy style that G avoids, and this varies hugely across specialist seeds. That means outcome-type stats from a single seed per run are fragile. EV, entropy, KL and return_var are reproducible.
findings.evidence: Duel self-play draw rate in the last window: S 0.230 versus G 0.007 (-0.222 [-0.238,-0.210]); S's draw rate rises from 0.05 to about 0.27 between 0.5M and 3.5M. Duel specialist seeds 0/1/2, last 0.52M: draw rate 0.230/0.445/0.019, game length 143/103/186, head-to-head deaths 0.61/1.01/0.24. In contrast EV 0.222/0.178/0.201, entropy 0.249/0.245/0.249, return_var 0.054/0.052/0.053, approx_kl all about 0.001. S duel against the heuristic ends 50/85/121 (33% draws) versus G 84/0/172 (G-S score -0.033 +/- 0.074). The G-S constrictor differences in draws, death causes and game length could therefore be partly seed idiosyncrasy, while the EV, entropy and return_var differences are well outside seed spread.

findings.claim: Q4 (logging trap): the top-level train fields in G's metrics.jsonl (explained_var, value_mean, games, mean_game_len, draws, deaths) are the first mode's (standard) only. Averaging or plotting them as 'G overall' misleads.
findings.evidence: Docstring of baselines/ppo_modes.py (HEADLINE_FIELDS) and chunk_record. Top-level loss, pg_loss, v_loss, entropy, approx_kl and clip_frac are mode-weighted means; the per-mode block 'game_modes' has everything per mode. I used the per-mode block throughout.

caveats: One training run per configuration (seed 0). CIs are block bootstraps over log records within a run, so they capture within-run noise and not seed-to-seed variation. The 3 duel-specialist seeds show EV, entropy, KL and return_var reproduce within a few percent, but outcome stats (draw rate 0.02-0.45, game length 103-186, head-to-head deaths) vary enormously. G-S differences in draws, death causes and game length (including constrictor's) may be partly seed idiosyncrasy.

Everything here is correlational. There is no ablation of value_norm, no equal-weight G, and no constrictor 16-minibatch specialist. The link from the 0.30 value weight to the explained-variance stall and slow early survival learning is a hypothesis, supported only by timing and magnitude. The EV decomposition (about 60-75% from lower G return variance) uses v_loss = 0.5*MSE and EV = 1 - MSE/return_var, which reproduces the logged EV within about 0.005. v_loss includes value clipping and post-update values, so the split is approximate.

Train-time diagnostics are stochastic-policy self-play (four copies of the same net), while evals are greedy play against heuristics. They need not agree: G's constrictor self-play keeps improving (self-collision slope -0.10 per 1M steps) while its eval against heuristics is flat. The head-to-head deficit against S (0.406) cannot be seen in any of these statistics.

G has 16 minibatches and S has 8. approx_kl and clip_frac are means per gradient step with different minibatch sizes, so G-S comparisons of them are confounded. The royale and standard 16-minibatch controls (S16 KL about 2.1x S8) are the proper reference; none exists for constrictor, and the duel one has barely started. royale-m16 had 155 of 160 records when read, so I used records 80:144 only.

The eval tests (slopes, chi2, the 2.10/3.15M dip comparison) use the logged normal-approximation half-widths from 256 games. The dip comparison (-0.056 +/- 0.041) was chosen after looking at the data and has no multiple-comparison correction. The 5-point trend tests have little power: G constrictor's slope CI of +/-0.014 per 1M steps still allows gains of up to about 0.07 over the run. Eval points exist only at 1.05, 2.10, 3.15, 4.19 and 5.24M.

Top-level fields in train records (explained_var, value_mean, games, mean_game_len, draws, deaths) are the first mode's (standard) only. I used the per-mode game_modes block. Logged return_var, value_weight, explained_var and value_mean are means over the 4 iterations in each 32,768-step chunk; approx_kl, clip_frac and the losses are means over all gradient steps in the chunk. mean_game_len covers games that finished within the chunk, a slight short-game bias that applies equally to all runs.

The explanations of why value_weight is small (horizon and discounting) and of why G's constrictor return variance is lower than S's are inferences I did not test; the latter I left unresolved. I did not re-run any policies or touch any file under the repo, and used no git commands. This was pure JSON analysis.

investigate:gradients.summary: I measured gradients in the generalist (G) at its 1M, 2M, 3M, 4M and 5.24M snapshots, and once at the constrictor specialist's final params as a control. For each parameter set I collected fresh on-policy rollouts with the trainer's own make_rollout: 64 envs x 128 turns per mode, after 256 discarded warm-up turns from fresh resets. That gave 2 rollouts per snapshot, and 4 independent ones at 5.24M (seeds 0 and 1 pooled). GAE and value weights came from the trainer's own functions. I took the gradients of the policy-loss, value-loss and entropy terms of pm.group_loss per mode, at the current params, on blocks of 4 envs (16 independent blocks per rollout and mode). The count-weighted block mean reproduces jax.grad of the trainer's full-batch group loss to a relative error of 1e-6. Analyses: the requested rollout-1 x rollout-2 cosines and noise ceilings; a pooled, de-noised estimate of the cosine between the modes' expected gradients (rho, a U-statistic over blocks); and a bootstrap over env blocks for intervals. Bottom line: the hypothesis holds clearly for the value-loss gradient but cannot be tested for the policy-gradient term. For the value loss, the three food modes point the same way (rho about 0.66-0.87 early on, in the specialist control too), while constrictor is roughly orthogonal to them. By the final snapshot it actively conflicts with standard's. Royale is well aligned with standard and duel, and G's value fit is worse than the specialist's in constrictor but better in standard and royale. The policy-gradient term dominates the shared torso (its per-rollout norm is 22-54x the value term's), but at this sample size it is almost pure noise. The noise ceilings are about 0 (-0.45 to 0.28), royale's expected policy gradient is undetectable at most snapshots, and the raw constrictor-vs-royale difference is ~0 at every snapshot. So nothing here shows constrictor's policy gradient conflicting more than royale's, and nothing rules it out either. Separately, constrictor contributes the smallest gradient to every update (0.57-0.71 of the food modes' mean norm). All of this used about 40 minutes of compute on core 0.

findings.claim: Value-loss term: the food modes' expected value gradients line up with each other, while constrictor's is about orthogonal to them. Royale is much better aligned with standard and duel than constrictor is with the food modes, well beyond the noise ceiling, at most snapshots.
findings.evidence: All params, rho = disattenuated cosine between expected gradients (95% percentile bootstrap over env blocks, 1000 reps). Mean rho of constrictor vs the 3 food modes, then royale vs {standard, duel}, then the difference: 1M 0.04 [-0.39,0.38] vs 0.74 [0.43,1.09], diff -0.70 [-1.31,-0.33]. 2M 0.46 [0.27,0.71] vs 0.84 [0.47,1.45], diff -0.38 [-0.95,0.01]. 3M 0.10 [-0.23,0.44] vs 0.84 [0.53,1.41], diff -0.74 [-1.40,-0.31]. 4M 0.16 vs 0.54, diff -0.38 [-1.90,0.11]. Raw rollout-1 x rollout-2 cosine difference, constrictor-vs-food minus royale-vs-{standard,duel} (est +-1.96 bootstrap SE): -0.50 [-0.71,-0.29], -0.20 [-0.38,-0.02], -0.48 [-0.67,-0.28], -0.16 [-0.29,-0.03], and 5.24M pooled -0.20 [-0.33,-0.08]. Value-gradient noise ceilings are high (0.2-0.9), so these numbers are interpretable.

findings.claim: Over training, constrictor's value gradient goes from orthogonal to conflicting: at the final params it points against standard's and against the sum of the other three modes. Meanwhile the food modes' own value gradients decorrelate late in training (their shared component appears to have been learned).
findings.evidence: 5.24M, 4 rollouts pooled. Constrictor vs standard: raw cosine -0.31 [-0.43,-0.19], rho -0.83 [-2.03,-0.46]. rho of constrictor vs the sum of the other three: -0.62 [-2.22,-0.08] over all params, -0.43 [-0.74,-0.14] over the shared torso only, -0.68 [-1.99,-0.24] under Adam's preconditioner (nu taken from runner.npz). Food-pair value rho: 0.66 / 0.80 / 0.87 at 1M / 2M / 3M, then 0.06 [-0.49,1.02] at 4M and 0.19 [-0.68,1.97] at 5.24M.

findings.claim: The value-gradient pattern is a property of the tasks, not of G's training history: the constrictor specialist's params show the same structure.
findings.evidence: Constrictor specialist, final params, its own rollouts in all 4 modes, scored with G's 4-mode loss. Value rho among the food pairs 0.60 [0.55,0.66]; constrictor vs food 0.16 [0.03,0.34]; difference -0.44 [-0.59,-0.26]. Shared torso only: food pairs 0.89 [0.80,0.97] vs constrictor-vs-food -0.05 [-0.36,0.33].

findings.claim: This matches a value-function deficit specific to constrictor: G fits values better than the specialists in standard and royale but worse in constrictor.
findings.evidence: explained_var, mean over the last ~1M env steps of the train records (each network on its own self-play data), G vs specialist: standard 0.234 vs 0.112; royale 0.284 vs 0.154; duel 0.167 vs 0.211; constrictor 0.219 vs 0.362. My measurement rollouts agree: G at 5.24M constrictor 0.23-0.24 (4 rollouts) vs the constrictor specialist's 0.32 (2 rollouts). value_norm also weights constrictor's value loss at 0.28-0.32 against 1.0-1.6 for the food modes (its return variance is 0.17 vs 0.03-0.05). This is an inference I did not test causally: the shared value head serves constrictor worst, which would give it poorer baselines.

findings.claim: Policy-gradient term: no detectable difference between constrictor and royale in raw cross-mode alignment at any snapshot. Every raw cross-mode cosine is near zero.
findings.evidence: All params, raw rollout-1 x rollout-2 cosines (est +-1.96 SE). Constrictor-vs-food minus royale-vs-{standard,duel}: 1M -0.06 [-0.20,0.08]; 2M 0.00 [-0.11,0.11]; 3M 0.01 [-0.15,0.17]; 4M -0.01 [-0.17,0.16]; 5.24M pooled 0.01 [-0.05,0.06]; 5.24M under Adam's metric -0.01 [-0.02,0.01]. Every cross-mode pair lies within +-0.16. Torso-only and total-loss results are the same.

findings.claim: The question of whether constrictor's policy gradient conflicts beyond the noise ceiling cannot be answered at this sample size: the policy gradient of a whole 64x128 rollout is mostly noise in every mode.
findings.evidence: Policy-gradient noise ceilings, cos(g_a^1, g_a^2), range -0.45 to 0.28 over snapshots and modes (royale -0.29, -0.12, 0.24, 0.07, 0.00). Under Adam's metric at 5.24M they are 0.04 / 0.03 / -0.01 / 0.09. Pooled reliability of the 5.24M estimate (4 rollouts): standard 0.43, duel 0.22, royale -0.16 (no detectable signal), constrictor 0.30. The disattenuated rho is undefined in 72-95% of bootstrap replicates for the key comparisons. I infer roughly 16x more rollouts per snapshot would be needed. Since a trainer minibatch is 1/16 of a rollout, each training step's direction is overwhelmingly noise in all modes (inference).

findings.claim: The policy-gradient term dominates the shared torso gradient, so the clear value-gradient conflict has a small direct effect on the shared torso. It acts mainly through the shared value head and dense layer.
findings.evidence: Ratio of per-rollout torso gradient norms, policy-gradient term / value term (standard, duel, royale, constrictor): 1M 35/54/40/49, 3M 24/40/27/33, 5.24M pooled 28/39/41/30; under Adam's metric 14/15/18/13. On de-noised (signal) norms the policy-gradient term is still about 10-20x larger (e.g. 5.24M constrictor 0.040 vs 0.0035).

findings.claim: Constrictor contributes the smallest gradient to every update: its per-rollout gradient norm is about 0.6-0.7 of the food modes' mean at every snapshot.
findings.evidence: Total-loss norm over all params, constrictor / mean of the food modes: 0.71 [0.59,0.83] (1M), 0.60 [0.48,0.72] (2M), 0.70 [0.58,0.83] (3M), 0.57 [0.46,0.68] (4M), 0.66 [0.57,0.75] (5.24M pooled), 0.71 [0.63,0.80] under Adam's metric. These norms are mostly noise. Constrictor has the most valid samples per rollout (about 27-28k vs 24k), so its per-sample gradients are smaller.

findings.claim: Side observation: at the constrictor specialist's params, constrictor's expected policy gradient is clearly measurable and larger than at G's params.
findings.evidence: Constrictor policy-gradient signal norm: specialist 0.097 [0.075,0.117] (reliability 0.65, ceiling 0.35) vs G at 5.24M 0.040 [0.008,0.080] (reliability 0.30, ceiling 0.12). The two use different policies and self-play opponents, so I am not interpreting this further.

findings.claim: The method reproduces the trainer's loss exactly at the current params.
findings.evidence: Duel group: the count-weighted mean of block gradients matches jax.grad of pm.group_loss on the full batch (norm_adv on) with relative error 1.0e-6, cosine 1.000001. Max |approx_kl| over all blocks is 7e-10, so the PPO ratio is 1 and clipping is inactive.

caveats: Advantages are normalised over each mode's whole rollout batch; the trainer normalises per random minibatch (1/16), which has the same expectation. With that change the block-gradient mean equals jax.grad of the trainer's full-batch group_loss to a relative error of 1e-6.

Rollouts start from fresh resets plus 256 discarded warm-up turns, not the trainer's steady-state game mix. Measured mean game lengths match training (constrictor about 31 turns, royale about 155-165, standard 220-300).

Cosines are on raw gradients except one check under Adam's metric at 5.24M, which uses nu from the trainer's final runner.npz (an average of clipped minibatch gradients of the summed loss). Raw-gradient alignment is not the same as Adam update alignment. The gradient clip and Adam's momentum are not modelled.

Intervals come from a bootstrap that resamples 4-env blocks within each (rollout, mode); 1000 reps, 500 for the 4-rollout pooled data. Resampling duplicates bias noise-dominated statistics: they inflate norms and shrink split-half cosines. So split-half quantities are given as est +-1.96 bootstrap SE, and U-statistic quantities (rho, signal norm, reliability) as percentile intervals, which are approximate. A few percentile intervals do not contain the point estimate (e.g. the constrictor specialist's constrictor reliability 0.65 [0.34,0.59]). rho is undefined whenever an estimated squared expected-gradient norm comes out <= 0, and the share of such replicates is reported.

Two rollouts per snapshot (4 at 5.24M), seed-0 runs only. To stay within the ~40-minute budget I skipped the standard-specialist control and an extra 4-rollout run at 1M. Snapshots before 3M did not save block gradients, so they could not be pooled across seeds.

Constrictor-specialist control: its rollouts in the food modes are off-distribution (explained_var -0.55 to -0.07 there), so its food-mode gradients mean 'learn this mode', and the loss uses G's 4-mode config and value weights.

The mechanism is inferred, not tested: a value-function conflict through the shared value head and dense layer gives constrictor poorer advantage baselines. I did not measure the policy-gradient term's interference beyond noise; the data neither show nor exclude it.
explained_var comparisons between G and the specialists come from the training logs (each network on its own self-play data), not from a common evaluation set.
Compute used: about 40 minutes on core 0 (taskset -c 0). Nothing under /home/user/slinkydotcpp was modified, and benchmarks/modes.py was not run.

investigate:snapshots.summary: I ran all the requested snapshot cells for constrictor and royale, plus a constrictor round robin I added, all pinned to core 3. The royale cells are clean: G leads at every matched snapshot and both G and S rise monotonically. The constrictor cells are not. Head-to-head results swing from 0.13 to 0.72 between neighbouring snapshots, and a round robin of the ten policies shows this is mostly cyclic (rock-paper-scissors) structure, not noise. Against 3 heuristics, G's constrictor strength dips 1M to 3M (-0.074 +-0.043), recovers by 5.24M and ends flat (+0.017 +-0.044 net), while S climbs +0.141 +-0.046. G minus S is positive at 1M (+0.082) and negative at every later snapshot, but only significantly at 2M and 3M. So 'G is worse than S in constrictor' depends heavily on which opponent and which checkpoint you measure. It is not a clean trajectory crossover. All numbers come from one code fingerprint (git_dirty False). Each line's own cell results are in cells.jsonl. Compute was about 34 min of wall time summed over 70 cells, roughly half of that CPU because core 3 was shared. I did not cut royale to 256 games.

findings.claim: Royale is clean: G leads S at matched training at every snapshot, and G@2M already equals S_final.
findings.evidence: (c) G@k vs S@k, team share (parity 0.5), 512 games, Wilson 95%: 1.05M 0.545 [0.502,0.588]; 2.10M 0.646 [0.603,0.686]; 3.15M 0.678 [0.636,0.717]; 4.19M 0.706 [0.665,0.744]; 5.24M 0.701 [0.660,0.739]. (a) G@k vs S_final: 0.299, 0.480 [0.437,0.524], 0.640, 0.663, 0.701. G@2M is at parity with the fully trained specialist, using 2.5x fewer env steps per mode. Final G 358 wins / 2 ties / 152 losses.

findings.claim: In royale, both G and S improve monotonically against the fixed S_final. G's gains plateau after about 3M, and S is still improving at the end.
findings.evidence: Paired steps in G's team share vs S_final (cell (a), same games, normal 95% CI of per-game differences): 1M->2M +0.182 +-0.057, 2M->3M +0.159 +-0.061, 3M->4M +0.023 +-0.058, 4M->5.24M +0.038 +-0.058 (3M->5.24M +0.062 +-0.057). (b) S@k vs S_final: 0.239, 0.330, 0.409, 0.471 [0.428,0.514] (still below 0.5 at 4M). No regression anywhere in royale.

findings.claim: In constrictor, G's head-to-head share against S_final is non-monotone and swings widely across snapshots. G is above parity at 2M and 3M and below at 1M, 4M and the end.
Constrictor policy space is strongly intransitive (cyclic). A single-opponent head-to-head at the final checkpoint is a noisy measure of strength here.
findings.evidence: Round robin of the 10 policies G@1..5M and S@1..5M (45 pairs, first 512 games each, common random numbers). The best transitive fit d_ij = r_i - r_j leaves 73.6% of the squared deviations from parity unexplained. A Monte Carlo of a purely transitive truth with the measured per-pair sampling variances gives a residual of 0.029 (95% range 0.017-0.044), against 1.651 observed. There are 17 strict 3-cycles, each edge's 95% interval excluding 0.5. Example: G@2M beats S_final 0.634 as team share, S_final beats G@4M 0.675, G@4M beats G@2M 0.590. Extreme pairs: G@4M beats G@3M 0.961, S@5M beats S@4M 0.866. Matched pair G@2M vs S@2M = 0.377 (S wins), yet G@2M beats S_final 0.613.

findings.claim: Over the whole constrictor population, the final G is the strongest policy by average share. At matched k, S is ahead through 3M, and G is ahead at 4M and (marginally) at the end.
findings.evidence: Field score = mean team share against the 9 other policies, 95% cluster bootstrap over game ids (4000 resamples): G5 0.585 [0.572,0.599], S5 0.560 [0.545,0.575], S1 0.545, G4 0.545, S2 0.515, S4 0.490, G1 0.478, G2 0.470, S3 0.441, G3 0.371. Matched G@k minus S@k field score: 1M -0.066 [-0.085,-0.047], 2M -0.045 [-0.068,-0.022], 3M -0.070 [-0.085,-0.055], 4M +0.055 [+0.044,+0.066], 5.24M +0.025 [0.000,+0.050]. Cross-run field (G@k vs the five S snapshots and vice versa): G5 0.596 [0.580,0.612], S5 0.532 [0.515,0.549]. G5 beats S1..S4 (0.564, 0.746, 0.520, 0.737) and loses only to S_final (0.412 over 512 games). The G5-vs-S5 loss is partly a specific matchup. The field score is itself one summary of an intransitive game, so it is inferential, not a strength ranking.

findings.claim: Against 3 heuristics in constrictor, G dips, recovers and ends where it started (a stall). S rises mostly by 3M and keeps most of the gain.

The specialist overtakes G against heuristics between 1M and 2M, but the gap is only reliably nonzero at 2M and 3M. By 4M and 5.24M it is smaller than the noise. There is no clean overtaking point head-to-head.
findings.evidence: Paired G minus S vs 3 heuristics (share, normal 95% on per-game differences, n=512): 1M +0.082 +-0.044 (G ahead), 2M -0.047 +-0.043, 3M -0.109 +-0.045, 4M -0.030 +-0.046, 5.24M -0.041 +-0.046. Head-to-head at matched k (c), 1024 games: G 0.380 at 1M, 0.377 at 2M, 0.583 at 3M, 0.546 at 4M, 0.406 at 5.24M, so S leads at 1M, 2M and 5.24M, and G leads at 3M and 4M. The two measures disagree at 3M: G beats S head-to-head, yet S beats G by 0.109 vs heuristics.

findings.claim: Inference, not measured: the cyclic structure explains why constrictor is 'worse' for G but royale is not. Royale has a clean transitive ordering, so G's matched-training lead shows up in every measure. Constrictor mixes opponent-specific counters with a small real difference.
findings.evidence: Royale: all three cell families (a), (b), (c) are monotone and consistent. Constrictor: the same families disagree in sign across snapshots, and the round-robin residual is 25 times the transitive-noise level. This run does not test it. Each run is a single seed, so the snapshot-to-snapshot swings could also reflect seed-level noise in the policies. Only extra seeds or a larger opponent population would separate these.

caveats: One seed per run: G and S each come from a single training run (seed 0), so snapshot-to-snapshot swings in constrictor cannot be separated from seed-level variation in the policies themselves. Intervals reflect game sampling only, not training-run variance.

Wilson intervals treat share as a proportion over n games. The paired CIs are normal intervals on per-game differences (cells of a mode share game ids 0..n-1, so the pairing is valid). The round-robin bootstrap resamples game ids jointly across all cells and uses the first 512 games of each cell, including the 1024-game ones.

The field score and the transitive-fit residual are summaries of an intransitive game, not strength rankings. The field includes four earlier snapshots from the same run as each policy, which favours late snapshots (they beat their own run's early snapshots), so the same-run and cross-run fields can disagree. The cross-run field is reported too.
The 17 strict 3-cycles were identified without multiple-comparison correction (about 120 triples). The overall residual (1.65 vs 0.029 expected from noise) does not depend on that.

Contention: core 3 was shared with another benchmark process, so wall seconds in cells.jsonl roughly double the CPU time. Game outcomes are unaffected. Batched-inference rounding can flip rare near-tie moves between runs with different game counts.

Royale was run at 512 games, not 1024 as in constrictor. The royale-vs-heuristics cells were not run, per the task (they only exist in the trainer's 256-game evals). The royale G-vs-S result above is not a measurement against heuristics.
The mechanistic explanation for why the cycles are stronger in constrictor than in royale is an inference, not tested here.

investigate:tailprobe.summary: I tested whether the generalist G plays constrictor as if bodies will clear (tail-moving semantics). For each move I computed two flood fills: area_con, where every current body is a permanent wall, and area_std, a time-aware fill where a body cell with countdown c is passable at move ≥ c. Areas come from my own numpy fills, and I scored G's and S's greedy choices on the same states. A first pass on greedy G,S,G,S games showed that greedy constrictor games are deterministic once the start is fixed: 512 games contained only 95 distinct games. So the main data are 1024 + 512 + 512 sampled-play constrictor games (G,S,G,S; S×4; G×4), all distinct, plus 256 sampled royale and 256 sampled standard games as a contrast. Bottom line: the mechanism is real but small, and it does not explain the constrictor result. (1) In the rare decisions where the two fills disagree, G takes the tail-semantics move about twice as often as S (13% vs 7% at k=5). G also walks into pockets that are traps only under constrictor rules more often than S (8.7% vs 5.4%). (2) G's moves react to the countdown channels about 5 times as much as S's in constrictor, as much as they do in royale, and in the tail-moving direction. Making bodies look about to clear makes G worse; making them clear 5 turns later makes it slightly better. S barely reacts. (3) The impact is about +0.013 extra trap deaths per G seat per game, at most about 0.01 of the 0.094 head-to-head gap. G and S die equally often overall. (4) Side finding that matters most for the user's question: G's constrictor deficit only appears in fully greedy play from the fixed openings. With sampled play G gets 0.495 [0.466, 0.524]. With 3 sampled opening moves then greedy it gets 0.490 [0.461, 0.518]. In greedy play the deficit comes from a few deterministic game lines: from cardinal starts with G's two snakes on opposite sides, G scores 0.000 in all 16 distinct games. G's lead in royale (0.742) and standard (0.809) holds under sampled play. Verdict: supported as a weak mechanism, refuted as the explanation of the constrictor gap.

findings.claim: In decisions where tail-moving and constrictor semantics disagree, G follows tail semantics about twice as often as S. Such decisions are rare.
findings.evidence: Pooled over the sampled constrictor data (G,S,G,S + S×4 + G×4; 2048 games, 158,897 decisions). A decision is divergent when every move with the highest area_std has area_con at least k cells below the best. Rate of picking the area_std-best move, G vs S [95% CI], G−S: k=1, n=861: 0.237 vs 0.174, +0.063 [+0.035, +0.093]. k=3, n=595: 0.145 vs 0.108, +0.037 [+0.008, +0.066]. k=5, n=414: 0.130 [0.098, 0.165] vs 0.070 [0.047, 0.095], +0.060 [+0.027, +0.094]. k=10, n=257: 0.117 vs 0.062, +0.054 [+0.016, +0.096]. The sign is the same on each state distribution (G−S at k=5: G,S,G,S +0.062 [0.018, 0.108]; S×4 +0.061 [−0.024, 0.149]; G×4 +0.057 [0.000, 0.121]). Both policies still pick the area_con-best move 85–93% of the time. There are only about 0.2 divergent decisions per game.

findings.claim: G's excess trap moves in constrictor are concentrated in 'masked' traps: small pockets that tail-moving semantics would call roomy. The size of the excess depends on whose states are used.
findings.evidence: T=8: a trap move has area_con < 8 while another legal move has area_con ≥ 16; a masked trap also has area_std ≥ 16. G,S,G,S sampled (1024 games): all traps G 0.065 [0.059, 0.072] vs S 0.046 [0.040, 0.052], G−S +0.019 [+0.012, +0.026]. Masked traps: 0.087 [0.074, 0.100] vs 0.054 [0.043, 0.064], G−S +0.033 [+0.019, +0.048]. Plain traps: 0.053 vs 0.043, G−S +0.011 [+0.003, +0.019]. Masked minus plain difference: +0.023 [+0.007, +0.038] (pooled +0.015 [+0.004, +0.026]). The same holds for T=5 and T=12. On S self-play states G looks worse (masked +0.040 [0.020, 0.059]). On G self-play states there is no G deficit (all −0.003 [−0.010, +0.004]; masked −0.015 [−0.032, +0.001]).

findings.claim: area_con is the right ground truth in constrictor and area_std in royale and standard, so the trap definitions mean what they claim.
findings.evidence: Moves actually played with area_con < 8: the snake died within area_con+1 moves 81.8% of the time in constrictor (n=3717), and 76.8% (n=1549) even when area_std ≥ 16. The same masked case led to death only 8.6% of the time in royale (n=1164) and 6.5% in standard (n=1228). Constrictor is not 100% because dead snakes' bodies are removed.

findings.claim: G reads the countdown channels in constrictor as strongly as in royale and in the tail-moving direction; the constrictor specialist has learned to mostly ignore them.
findings.evidence: Greedy-move flip rate when only the countdown channels change, G vs S. Constrictor (79,019 decisions): 'far' (all bodies = max countdown) 0.101 vs 0.019; 'near' (all = 2/121) 0.111 vs 0.021; shift+5 turns 0.071 vs 0.013; shift+10 turns 0.132 vs 0.026. Royale, where countdowns are true (G vs the royale specialist): far 0.081 vs 0.067; shift+5 0.076 vs 0.061 (80-game subsample). Direction of the effect on G in constrictor: 'near' raises its trap rate by +0.042 [+0.035, +0.050], its rate of picking the area_std-best move at k=5 by +0.101 [+0.048, +0.154], and lowers its rate of picking the area_con-best move (decisions where area_con ranges ≥ 5) by −0.048. Shift+5 lowers G's trap rate by −0.009 [−0.014, −0.005] and its area_std-best rate by −0.031 [−0.059, −0.005], and raises its area_con-best rate by +0.007 [+0.003, +0.011]: about half of the G−S trap gap. S's changes are all ≤ 0.010. Positive control: in royale, shift+5 lowers the trap rate of both policies (G −0.026, S −0.029), the same direction. Offline recomputation matched the stored choices 100%.

findings.claim: The tail-semantics errors are far too small to explain G's constrictor head-to-head deficit.
findings.evidence: Death attribution in sampled G,S,G,S games (a trap move played within 12 turns before death): masked-trap deaths per seat-game G 0.028 [0.021, 0.036] vs S 0.016 [0.010, 0.021], G−S +0.013 [+0.004, +0.021]. Plain-trap deaths: −0.002 [−0.013, +0.010]. All deaths per seat: 0.782 vs 0.780, G−S +0.002 [−0.026, +0.032]. Rough bound (each extra death costs at most about 0.5 share): about 0.01 or less of the 0.094 gap (0.5 − 0.406).

findings.claim: Side finding: greedy G vs S in constrictor is deterministic given the start (48 start layouts × seat order). Here G's deficit is a few repeated game lines rather than a general weakness; with diverse openings G is at parity.
findings.evidence: My greedy harness, 512 games: 95 distinct games; G share 0.428 [0.388, 0.466] counting every game, 0.421 [0.332, 0.516] over the distinct games. Fully sampled play: 0.495 [0.466, 0.524] (1024 distinct games). First 3 turns sampled, then greedy: 0.490 [0.461, 0.518] (1024 games, 631 distinct; distinct only 0.515 [0.478, 0.551]). First turn sampled: 0.446 [0.417, 0.474] (only 189 distinct; distinct only 0.492 [0.421, 0.561]). Greedy distinct games by layout: cardinal starts with G's snakes opposite, share 0.000 (16 games); corners, opposite 0.267 (15); corners, adjacent 0.625 (32); cardinals, adjacent 0.500 (32). Royale sampled 0.742 [0.688, 0.793] and standard sampled 0.809 [0.762, 0.852], so G's lead in those modes is not a greedy artefact. Teammate head-on collisions do not explain it (G 69 vs S 115 in the sampled games).

findings.claim: G does partly adapt to constrictor: it takes masked pockets and tail-adjacent cells less there than in tail-moving modes, but less selectively than the specialists.
findings.evidence: Masked-trap rate (T=8, sampled G,S,G,S states), G / mode specialist: standard 0.132 / 0.101, royale 0.162 / 0.154, constrictor 0.087 / 0.054. Tail-adjacent move rate when only some legal moves touch the own tail, G / S: standard 0.514 / 0.418, royale 0.516 / 0.450, constrictor 0.394 / 0.393. These are cross-mode comparisons on different state distributions, so they are only suggestive.

caveats: Most results use states from sampled play (each seat samples from its own policy), because greedy constrictor play gives only ~95 distinct games per 512. The benchmark plays greedy, so its state distribution differs. On the 95 distinct greedy games the trap and divergence differences have the same sign but tiny n (e.g. k=1: n=47).

area_std uses a time-aware fill where only the newest frontier expands (the heuristic's default). The 'wait' variant is useless in constrictor: every body eventually 'opens', so every move scores ~121. Neither fill models eating, other snakes' future heads, head-to-heads or growth. area_con ignores growth and the removal of dead snakes' bodies, which is why only ~82% of played constrictor traps end in death within area_con+1 moves rather than 100%.

Divergent decisions in the task's argmax sense are rare in constrictor (~0.2 per game), because area_std is usually the whole board for every move. In royale and standard they are nearly absent (n ≤ 29), so the argmax contrast has no power there. The masked-trap comparison carries the contrast instead.
The G−S differences in trap rates depend on whose states are used: G is worse on S's own states and not worse on G's own states. A 50/50 mix gives a moderate G deficit.

The countdown changes are out-of-distribution inputs; constrictor tails always show countdown 2. 'far' and 'near' also destroy the ordering along each body, which the network may use for shape and direction. The shift variants preserve it. Read flip rates as sensitivity, not as an exact causal effect of 'belief about clearing'.

All CIs are percentile bootstraps over games (B=2000), with ratio-of-sums estimators; G−S CIs are paired on the same resample. Decisions within a game are correlated; the game-level resampling accounts for that. In the deduplicated greedy data, some distinct games are mirror images of each other, so even 95 overstates the effective n.

The share comparisons with sampled or partly sampled openings measure different policies than the benchmark's fully greedy agents. They show the greedy deficit does not survive diverse openings, not that the benchmark number is wrong for its exact setting. I did not inspect the benchmark's own per-game list. My greedy harness reproduced 0.428, close to the benchmark's 0.406, and the benchmark may rotate seats differently (at most ~192 distinct games).
The 'impact' bound (≤ ~0.01 share) is a back-of-envelope conversion from the extra masked-trap deaths per seat-game. It is not a measured counterfactual.

The benchmark record also shows G dying 252 times by wall collision versus 0 for S, and more often in head-on collisions (689 vs 533). I did not investigate this; wall deaths likely occur when no safe move exists, so they say little about blunders.

Compute: about 40 minutes in total on core 2 under taskset, except one unpinned analysis command of mine. I stopped that command with TaskStop. No other process was touched, and nothing under the repo was modified.

investigate:behaviour.summary: I replayed the benchmark's G,S,G,S constrictor and royale games exactly (per-game shares and placements match benchmarks/results/modes.jsonl with max abs diff 0.0), recorded every decision state, death, killer and both policies' counterfactual moves, and analysed them with game-level cluster bootstrap CIs. Bottom line. (1) The greedy constrictor head-to-head (G 0.406) is only 12 distinct deterministic games repeated (G 4 wins / 2 draws / 6 losses = 5/12 = 0.417 exactly), so its reported +-0.03 CI is meaningless. (2) The deficit is nonetheless real in near-greedy play: with 2% random legal moves (1524 distinct games of 2048) G share is 0.417 [0.396, 0.437]. It shrinks monotonically with action noise (5%: 0.438, 10%: 0.461) and is gone under full sampling (0.488 [0.468, 0.508]). Royale shows G ahead (0.70) greedy or sampled. (3) In the near-greedy regime G loses constrictor games almost entirely through games that contain a head-on collision. Head-ons are always mutual kills (equal lengths), and in games whose first head-on is a G-vs-S one (34% of games) G scores 0.31; with no head-on (55%) G scores 0.48, near parity. Constrictor removes the length lever that wins G its royale head-ons (G is longer in about 73-75% of royale G-S head-ons). Most opening/style differences are real and large but are not by themselves a strength difference, since under sampling G and S are equal despite the same differences. Causal attribution beyond this is inference.

findings.claim: The greedy G-vs-S constrictor result rests on only 12 distinct games, so the benchmark's CI is not a sampling CI.
findings.evidence: Constrictor with greedy policies and hidden food is deterministic given the start. 4 snakes start on either all 4 corners or all 4 cardinal points (48 ordered placements); with 2 seat parities that gives 96 (placement, parity) configs, and snakes of a team are interchangeable, leaving 2 start sets x 6 choices of which two start cells G holds = 12 distinct games. In my 512 games (first 512 of the benchmark cell) every config appears (96 distinct trajectories) and every group of 8 is identical in action sequences and outcome (verified in orbits.py). Exact population value: G wins 4, draws 2, loses 6, G share 5/12 = 0.4167 (corner starts 0.500, cardinal starts 0.333). Start-level bootstrap over the 48 placements: 0.417 [0.312, 0.521]; sign test over placements (16 G-ahead vs 24 G-behind): p = 0.27. The benchmark's 1024 games (0.406, 327/177/520) are the same 12 games repeated about 85 times each. G vs 3 heuristics is not affected: 256 distinct trajectories out of 256 games for both G and S, because the heuristic breaks ties randomly. caveats: Greedy constrictor G-vs-S has only 12 distinct games, so any statistic from the benchmark protocol itself (including my 'greedy' 512-game and 96-game runs) cannot support a hypothesis test; they are exact descriptions of those 12 games. All inferential statements use the eps-noise and sampled runs, which are different (noisier) policies than the benchmark's greedy ones. The eps=0.02 result is continuous with the exact greedy value (0.417 vs 0.417) but this continuity is an observation, not a proof.

Everything is one training seed per agent (generalist seed 0, each specialist seed 0). Bootstrap CIs are over games, so they reflect game sampling noise, not seed-to-seed training variation; a 'beyond noise' difference here means beyond game-sampling noise for these two networks.

Only the 4-snake constrictor and royale G,S,G,S cells were examined (royale greedy 256 games = first 256 of the benchmark's 1024; constrictor greedy 512 = first 512 of 1024). Royale games are stochastic (food, hazard sides) so game-level bootstrap is valid there; I did not check whether the 96 (placement, parity) start configs bias royale.

Interval multiplicity: per-move survival and per-turn opening series show 'significant' marks at many individual moves; with about 54 moves some stars (about 5%) are expected by chance. I flagged only moves where the difference is large and persists across neighbouring moves (survival moves 18-20 and 35-40). Late-game statistics (t>=10 centre distance, wall distance, territory) are conditioned on a snake still being alive and are survivorship-biased.

Death-cause labels for non-head-on deaths (wall/self/other body) are arbitrary choices among doomed moves (mask all-True, no safe move): do not read them as skill. 'Forced' is as defined by slinky.rules.action_mask (no move that is not certainly fatal), which is exactly what the policy is masked by.

Voronoi territory and flood-fill 'room' are my own proxies (4-neighbour BFS over empty cells, ties neutral, tails never free in constrictor, other snakes held at their current heads; the delay-1 handicap for the mover in the lookahead). They are descriptive and not validated against optimal play; the claim that G's colliding snake is worse placed is observational, not a controlled test.

Contested view = deaths counted while snakes of both policies were alive at the start of the move (the benchmark's early-stop rule); the full-game view includes the intra-team fights after the contest is decided and is shown only in the output files. 'Draw' = the contest ended with nobody alive and >=2 snakes eliminated on the last move, equal to the benchmark's ties (94 of 512 greedy games = benchmark ties; royale 1 of 256).

The hybrid splice experiment (hybrid.py, greedy) is non-monotone and uninterpretable because it only has 12 distinct games; I report it only as a warning, not as evidence for or against an opening effect. A well-powered version would need noise (eps-greedy or sampled) at each K and about 30-45 s per K per 1024 games.

Compute: about 20-25 minutes pinned to core 1 (simulations roughly 15 minutes: 2048 games of constrictor take about 75 s, 512 royale about 70 s; plus about 5 minutes of numpy analysis). No files outside my directory were touched; no processes outside my own were signalled; benchmarks/modes.py was not run, so no results file was written. benchmarks/modes.py's cell_key is copied into simulate.py (not imported).

## Why G looks worse in constrictor but good in royale

**Short version.** Most of the "worse in constrictor" result comes from how it was measured. The robust finding is that G has **no edge** in constrictor, while it has a large one in royale. The best-supported reason for that asymmetry is that G's royale edge is built from skills it shares with standard and duel: eating to be longer, winning head-on collisions by length, and surviving long games. Constrictor has none of those levers, and it shares little learning signal with the other modes. There is also a small residual deficit in near-greedy play, and some signs that multi-mode training slowed G's constrictor learning mid-run, but neither has been shown to cause the 0.406.

### 1. The 0.406 is 12 games, not 1024 (established)
Two investigations (behaviour and tailprobe) found this independently.
- In constrictor, food is inert, so greedy-vs-greedy play is fully determined by the start.
- There are 2 start layouts (the four corners or the four edge midpoints) and 6 ways to give G two of the four cells: 12 distinct games.
- G wins 4, draws 2 and loses 6, so its share is 5/12 = 0.417. The benchmark's 1024 games are those 12 repeated about 85 times, so its ±0.03 interval means nothing.
- A bootstrap over start placements gives [0.31, 0.52]; a sign test over placements gives p = 0.27.
- G loses both games where its two snakes start on opposite edge midpoints.

### 2. Measured without that problem, G is level in constrictor and far ahead in royale (established)
**Constrictor:**
- Fully sampled play: G share 0.488 [0.468, 0.508] over 2048 games (behaviour), and 0.495 [0.466, 0.524] over 1024 games with independent keys (tailprobe).
- Three sampled opening moves, then greedy: 0.490 [0.461, 0.518].
- Against 3 heuristics, paired over the benchmark's 1024 games: G−S = −0.012 [−0.044, +0.022]. I bootstrapped this myself from benchmarks/results/modes.jsonl.

**Royale:**
- Head to head: 0.697 greedy, 0.706 and 0.742 sampled.
- Against heuristics: G−S = +0.176 [+0.140, +0.213].
- G leads S at every matched snapshot (0.55 to 0.71), and G at 2M steps already equals the final S.

### 3. The remaining near-greedy deficit sits mostly in the fixed greedy game lines (supported; my reanalysis of the behaviour team's eps-greedy games)
At eps = 0.02 (a random legal move 2% of the time), G scores 0.417 overall.
- 41% of those games never leave a greedy line before the contest ends, and G scores 0.404 [0.373, 0.436] in them.
- Games with a random move in the first 10 moves give G 0.463 [0.430, 0.495].
- With eps 0.05 or 0.10 and an early random move, G scores 0.457 and 0.467 (the intervals just exclude 0.5).

So something like 0 to 0.04 of the 0.094 gap may be a general near-greedy weakness. The rest belongs to a few start configurations.

How G loses those lines (descriptive, not causal):
- Head-on collisions in constrictor always kill both snakes, because every snake has the same length.
- Games whose first head-on is G against S give G a share of 0.31.
- Games with a G-G teammate head-on (6.2% of games, against 4.5% for S-S) give G 0.01.

### 4. Why royale and not constrictor (supported, the causal link partly inferred)
**What royale's edge is made of (measured):**
- G's snakes are longer from move 25 to 75 (+0.3 segments).
- G survives 73-77% of the head-on collisions between a G and an S snake that leave a survivor, and it is the longer snake in about 75% of them.
- More G snakes are still alive at moves 100-200 (+0.17 to +0.33 of seats).
- G has fewer deaths with no safe move (16.5% vs 28.1% of seats).

In constrictor all snakes always have equal length, there is no food, and games last about 30 turns, so none of these levers exist.

**How much the modes share (measured by the gradients investigation):**
- The value-loss gradients of standard, duel and royale point the same way (de-noised cosine 0.66-0.87 at 1-3M steps).
- Constrictor's is roughly orthogonal to them (0.04 to 0.46; about 0.1 at 3M).
- At the final snapshot it points against standard's (cosine −0.83 [−2.03, −0.46]).
- The same pattern appears at the constrictor specialist's own parameters, so it is a property of the tasks, not of G's training history.

**Supporting signs:**
- G learned royale faster from the start: fewer self-collisions by 1M steps, and G at 2M equals the final S.
- Extra gradient steps don't explain it: a 16-minibatch royale specialist scores 0.166 against heuristics, below the 8-minibatch one (0.216) and far below G (0.341).

**Still inferred:**
- That shared structure is *why* G gains in royale and not in constrictor.
- The policy-gradient part, which dominates the shared network body, was too noisy to measure at the sample sizes used.

**A wrinkle:** specialists transfer to a new mode without retraining no better into royale than into constrictor. The standard specialist scores 0.098 in royale and 0.108 in constrictor. So "royale is close to standard" holds for what the value function has to learn, not for the policy as a whole.

### 5. G gave constrictor a thin slice of training and learned it unevenly (suggestive; one seed; causal role untested)
- **Value-loss weight:** G scales each mode's value loss by the inverse of its return variance. That gives constrictor a weight of 0.30, against 1.1-1.5 for the other modes (7% of the total).
- **Gradient size:** constrictor's contribution to each update is the smallest of the four, 0.57-0.71 of the other modes' average.
- **Early survival:** G had about 0.24 more self-collision deaths per game than S until about 2.6M steps, despite twice as many gradient updates.
- **Eval curve:** G's score against heuristics dipped from 1M to 3M steps (−0.074 ± 0.043, replicated on independent games) and then recovered. S climbed by +0.141 ± 0.046.
- **Who led when:** S was clearly ahead of G only at 2-3M steps (−0.109 ± 0.045 at 3M).
- **Net:** by 5.24M steps none of this leaves G behind against heuristics.

### 6. G partly plays constrictor as if tails moved (supported as a mechanism, refuted as the explanation)
- G's moves react to the "turns until this body cell frees" channels about 5 times as much as S's in constrictor, where those cells never free.
- In the rare decisions where the two space counts disagree, G picks the move that is only roomy if tails move twice as often as S does (13% vs 7%).
- The cost is about 0.013 extra trap deaths per G seat per game, worth at most about 0.01 of share.

### Refuted or weakened
- **Mode confusion:** telling G the wrong mode changes only 2-6% of its moves.
- **Extra gradient steps:** the 16-minibatch controls rule this out (section 4).
- **A broken constrictor value function:** G's value error is only 6% above S's. 60-75% of its lower explained variance comes from its returns being less variable, so the gradients report's "worse value fit" overstates it.
- **Opening style as the cause:** the same style differences persist under sampling, where G ties.
- **Strong rock-paper-scissors cycles among snapshots (the snapshots report):** its test assumed 512 independent games per pair. With 12 distinct games, a purely transitive ordering would leave a residual of 1.21 [0.72, 1.84] against the 1.65 observed (p ≈ 0.075). The cycles, and the swings from 0.13 to 0.72 between snapshots, are what 12 chaotic games look like.

The quoted '6%' and the top of '60-75%' come from the last window, where G's return_var hits its lowest value of all windows (0.165, against 0.170-0.176 before). More importantly, the decomposition rests on an implausible counterfactual: G's MSE held fixed while its return variance rises to S's. MSE is not independent of return variance. In the units that matter for a baseline, the variance removed by the value function is var − MSE = 0.036 for G vs 0.069 for S. G's value function removes about half as much return variance as S's. 'Not much worse in absolute terms' is therefore a framing choice, not a finding. Both are also measured on each network's own self-play data, not a common set.

Re-running synthesis/rr_neff.py reproduces: observed residual 1.651; n_eff = 12 null mean 1.214, 95% range [0.715, 1.839], P = 0.075. With n_eff = 512 the null is 0.029, which is the snapshots report's error. 'Not established, not ruled out' is the right conclusion. The test has little power at 12 games, and the normal noise model for outcomes in {0, 0.5, 1} is approximate. Two individual extremes are large under a per-pair SE of 0.13: S@4M vs S_final at 0.132 (z ≈ −2.9) and G@4M vs G@3M at 0.961 (z ≈ +3.5). They are covered by the joint null, but 'what 12 chaotic games look like' slightly understates how unusual they are. Within the exact 12-game population the cycles are real; whether to treat the starts as a sample is a modelling choice, as the claim says.

Table B and the aftermath numbers reproduce from the behaviour outputs. Three problems. (1) 'G has more deaths with no safe move (49.4% vs 41.7%)' is an identity, not a mechanism. Forced = 100 − alive − head-on with opponent − head-on with teammate (G 49.4 + 21.1 + 6.2 + 23.2; S 41.7 + 21.1 + 4.5 + 32.7). It just restates that G loses more often. (2) The G-G teammate cost of −0.030 is largely cancelled by S-S at +0.022, so the net teammate effect is only about −0.008. In the full-game view the teammate pattern reverses (G 6.6% vs S 8.7%), as it does in sampled play. (3) 'First head-on type' is a post-treatment bucket. The territory gap before G-S collisions (4.27 vs 6.99) is descriptive, and the conversion table is odd: G with a lead of 3 or more cells still scores only 0.317. The 'suggestive' label is appropriate, but the forced-death sentence should go.

No ablation tests it (no 3-mode G, no equal value weights, no transfer test). Several of its pillars are weaker than stated: C5's survival lever is circular, C6's torso-level value gradients are aligned with the food modes at 2-3M, C9's direction evidence is mixed, and C14's wrong-mode interval allows about 0.07. A simpler alternative is not considered: the specialists' headroom. Constrictor games last about 32 turns against about 170 in royale, so the constrictor specialist sees roughly 5x more episodes for the same env steps. Its vs-heuristic curve plateaus from 3M (trainer evals 0.230/0.230/0.234; snapshot cell (d) 0.240/0.237/0.264). The royale and standard specialists are still improving or very weak (royale S@4M vs S_final 0.471; standard S 0.028 vs heuristics). 'G helps where the specialist is data-starved, and constrictor's specialist is not' fits the same data without invoking shared structure or interference.

'G told standard 0.225 = told constrictor 0.225' compares a 256-game cell with the full 1024-game cell, and the match is a coincidence. On the same 256 game ids (cell_key depends only on seed and mode), G told constrictor scores 0.245 and G told standard, duel and royale score 0.225, 0.206 and 0.221. Paired differences: −0.020 [−0.070, +0.031], −0.040 [−0.080, −0.001], −0.024 [−0.068, +0.022]. Pooled wrong-mode effect: −0.028 [−0.069, +0.009] (verify-statistics/c14_wrongmode.py). All three point estimates are negative, and the interval allows a drop of up to 0.07 (about 28% of a 0.245 score). 'No detectable effect; a small one is not excluded' is supported; 'not its strength (established)' is not. The 2-6% move-change figure comes from the task context and I did not recompute it. 'Mode confusion' in the broader sense of cross-mode semantics leaking into constrictor is exactly what C9 proposes, so C14 rules out only the mode flag.

With the 12 games as the unit, the bootstrap gives [0.17, 0.67] and the sign test (4 vs 6) gives p = 0.75. Script: verify-statistics/c1_n12.py.

Answer section 4 says 'G's snakes are longer from move 25 to 75'. It omits that S's living snakes are longer at moves 150-200 (−0.75 and −1.14), and that the pooled difference is +0.12 [−0.03, +0.26]. 'More G snakes alive' and 'fewer no-safe-move deaths' restate the outcome and are not mechanisms.

Answer section 5 lists duel's value weight under '1.1-1.5 for the other modes'; it is 0.96-1.08. The self-collision excess is presented as worse 'early survival', but it is offset by fewer head-on deaths in the same windows. Total deaths are equal; only game length (−2 turns) measures survival.

The contradictions item calls the snapshot dip test 'not chosen after looking at that data'. This cannot be verified: 1M→3M is exactly the trough of the snapshot data itself. The dip survives a Bonferroni correction over 10 pairwise snapshot contrasts (z ≈ 3.4), but it describes checkpoints of a single seed.

Selective highlighting across many comparisons: k=5 of four divergence thresholds, the standard pair of three at 5.24M, the shift+5 counterfactual where shift+30 points the opposite way, and t = 25-75 of the length curve. An untested alternative explanation is missing from the synthesis: specialist headroom. The constrictor specialist gets about 5x more episodes per env step (games of about 32 turns vs about 170) and plateaus against heuristics from 3M. The royale and standard specialists are still improving or very weak.
