verdicts.reason: The core claim is right. orbits.py reruns to 12 groups of 8 identical games, G 4 wins / 2 draws / 6 losses, 5/12 = 0.417, and G loses both opposite-edge-midpoint games. But the quoted uncertainty makes the same pseudo-replication error the claim criticises. The [0.31, 0.52] interval and p = 0.27 come from extra_constrictor.py's bootstrap and sign test over 48 placements (16 vs 24). Each placement averages two complementary games, and only 6 distinct complementary pairs exist, so the 16 vs 24 is just 4x(4 vs 6). Recomputed (verify-method/c1_ci.py, 20000 resamples): bootstrap over the 12 games gives [0.17, 0.67]. Over the 6 complementary pairs (each policy plays each side) it gives [0.125, 0.71], with G ahead 2, level 1, behind 3. Exact sign test: 4 vs 6 games p = 0.75; over pairs p = 1.0. One corner pair is decided by position alone (the x=9 side wins whoever holds it). The conclusion that 0.406 is uninformative gets stronger, not weaker, but the reported CI and p are wrong. Also, the ±0.03 is a valid sampling CI for this fixed protocol's mean. It is meaningless about general strength, not about sampling.

The cited numbers check out. My paired bootstrap of the benchmark G,H,H,H vs S,H,H,H cells gives -0.012 [-0.044, +0.022] (4000 resamples over game ids; valid pairing, because cell_key depends only on seed and mode). But 'level under non-degenerate protocols' is selective. The eps-greedy runs are non-degenerate (2000 and 2047 distinct games of 2048), yet G is behind: 0.438 [0.418, 0.458] at eps 0.05 and 0.461 [0.440, 0.481] at eps 0.10. At eps 0.10, 92% of games had a random move in the first 10 moves and still give 0.467 [0.445, 0.488]. Parity holds only for temperature-1 sampling and 3 sampled opening moves. Tailprobe's 1-sampled-move protocol gives 0.446 [0.417, 0.474]. The vs-heuristic interval allows a -0.044 deficit (about 18% of parity 0.25). Its first 512 games give -0.041 [-0.086, +0.006] and its second 512 give +0.018. So: no detectable difference under sampling; not established as 'level' near greedy.

The royale lead holds in every measurement I checked, but one number in the claim is wrong. The 'vs heuristics G-S +0.176 [+0.140, +0.213]' is G minus the 16-minibatch specialist S16: I get G-S16 = +0.1755 [0.139, 0.212]. G minus the 8-minibatch S is +0.125 [+0.087, +0.161] (paired bootstrap over 1024 benchmark game ids, verify-method/bench_pairs.py). It is +0.143 on the first 512 games and +0.107 on the second 512, consistent with diagnostics' +0.133 ± 0.042. The synthesis apparently matched the S16,H,H,H row. Also, the matched snapshots are not strictly monotone (0.706 at 4M, 0.701 at 5.24M): they plateau. Royale games are stochastic (256 of 256 distinct), so game-level CIs are valid. One seed per run.

I reran synthesis/eps_split.py and it reproduces. Implementation checks out: applied moves come from the same forward pass as the recorded greedy ag / a_s (simulate.py), so act != own means an effective random move. Interpretation problems: (1) The buckets are not monotone in how early the perturbation came. At eps 0.02, a first random move at moves 0-2 gives 0.444 [0.391, 0.496] (balanced over who deviated: 0.443), and at moves 3-9 gives 0.476. So the earliest perturbation leaves a deficit of about 0.056. (2) Tailprobe's first-turn-sampled-then-greedy run gives 0.446 [0.417, 0.474], also about a 0.05 deficit. (3) The no-deviation bucket selects short contests, and late-deviation buckets (0.370, 0.323) select long ones, so bucket differences mix line identity with contest length. (4) Random moves dilute any general skill gap toward 0.5, which by itself makes early-perturbed games look closer to parity. The descriptive split is correct. The 'residual 0 to 0.04' is narrower than the data allow: about 0.01-0.06.

The royale statistics are as reported. The inference that constrictor has none of these levers is partly contradicted. (1) 'G survives 73-77% of G-S head-ons' and 'G is longer in 73-75%' are one fact: under standard and royale rules the strictly longer snake always survives, so these are not two levers. (2) The fewer no-safe-move deaths lever (16.5% vs 28.1% of seats) is trap avoidance, which does exist in constrictor, where forced deaths are the main way to die. There G shows no edge: +7.8pp more forced deaths at eps 0.02 (behaviour Table D), and all deaths per seat 0.782 vs 0.780 under sampling (tailprobe). So a skill G has in royale fails to transfer to constrictor even though constrictor rewards it. That argues against 'constrictor lacks the levers' as the whole story. (3) The length comparison at t=25-75 is among living snakes (survivorship-conditioned). The length and head-on levers are genuinely absent in constrictor (equal lengths verified).

The method itself looks sound: the value term is per-sample independent across 4-env blocks, so the U-statistic is unbiased. But the interpretation is weaker than stated. From the gradients team's 'full' arrays (verify-method/vgrad_bias.py, split-half raw cosines): (1) 83-99% of the value-term squared gradient norm sits in the 257-parameter value head, so 'constrictor is roughly orthogonal' is mainly about the linear readout. (2) Restricted to the shared torso (conv + hidden), constrictor's value gradient lines up substantially with the food modes at G 2M (raw cosine C vs food 0.50, against food pairs 0.63) and 3M (0.38 vs 0.60). Disattenuated, that is about 0.6, not orthogonal. The separation is clear only at 1M (0.02 vs 0.18) and at the specialist's parameters. (3) The specialist control does not show 'a property of the tasks'. Its food-mode rollouts are off-distribution (EV -0.55 to -0.07). Its value-head bias gradients have the same sign in all food modes and are large in duel and royale (-0.009, -0.016), so the food modes share one miscalibration, which by itself aligns their gradients (torso food pairs 0.86). (4) The rho intervals go far outside [-1, 1] (e.g. -0.83 [-2.03, -0.46]), so rho is unstable. The raw cosine -0.31 [-0.43, -0.19] is the reliable figure for the late conflict with standard.

Verified in modes.jsonl. S16 royale vs 3 heuristics is 0.1655 over 1024 games. It was benchmarked at 17:46 from the final params.npz, written 17:38 after all 160 records, so it is not a partial run. Paired over the same games: S - S16 = +0.051 [+0.018, +0.084] and G - S16 = +0.176 [+0.139, +0.212]. Head to head, S16 vs S gives S16 0.456 and G vs S16 gives G 0.717. The EV and self-death numbers match diagnostics' m16 table. Caveat: one seed per configuration, and duel seeds show outcome stats can vary a lot across seeds, but the G gap is far larger than the S8-S16 gap.

The value weights and eval numbers are correct, but two pieces are misread. (1) Self-collision deaths are not a survival measure in 4-copy self-play. Deaths per game are fixed at about 3.1 for both runs (windows.json: G-S total deaths -0.02 to -0.04). G's early +0.24 self deaths are offset by -0.31 head-on deaths, and behaviour showed every non-head-on constrictor death is forced (the wall/self/body label is just which doomed move gets picked). So this shows a death-mix and style difference: G was trapped more and collided head-on less, with shorter games by about 2 turns. It does not directly show slower survival learning. (2) 'Despite twice as many gradient updates' misleads (ppo_modes docstring). Each G step takes 1/16 of each group, so half of an S minibatch's constrictor samples, and constrictor's policy loss carries weight 1/4. Per epoch, constrictor's raw pre-Adam push is about half the specialist's, not double. (3) The gradient norms cited are noise-dominated (the gradients report says so). (4) Using 3M as the trough of the dip is a post-hoc choice on the snapshot data, though the trainer's independent evals show the same 2-3M low. One seed; suggestive at most.

The mechanism holds up. I checked whether G is simply less peaked: binned by masked top-2 logit margin (verify-method/flip_margin.py, 81,240 decisions with 2+ legal moves), G still flips far more under countdown-only changes. 'far': G 0.110 vs S 0.022, or 0.026 with S reweighted to G's margin distribution. 'near': 0.120 vs 0.027. At margin 2-3, G 0.131 vs S 0.006. But the impact bound does not support 'refuted as the explanation'. (1) It is measured in sampled play, where G is already level with S (0.495) and all deaths per seat are equal, so there is no gap there to explain. (2) In the near-greedy regime that carries the deficit, G has +7.8pp more forced (trapped) deaths per seat (behaviour, eps 0.02), and nobody split those by masked vs plain traps. (3) The back-of-envelope uses 0.5 share per death. With 2 G seats, +0.013 per seat could be worth up to about 0.026 if a death flips a win to a loss. (4) Attribution needs a trap move within 12 turns of death, which misses indirect effects.

The arithmetic is right, but the mechanism is wrong. The trainer's return_var is the variance of GAE(0.95) returns = advantages + V (ppo_modes.py lines 1053-1077; compute_gae returns adv + values), so it depends on the critic. Tests: (1) On tailprobe's sampled self-play (512 games each), Monte Carlo discounted placement returns have the same variance for G×4 and S×4: 0.342 vs 0.349, G-S -0.0065 [-0.013, +0.0003]. With V≡0 the lambda-return variance is 0.150 vs 0.150 (verify-method/mc_retvar.py). (2) With the trainer's own rollout code (32 envs × 1920 turns per policy after 96 warm-up turns; verify-method/value_mc.py, value_mc_out.txt): G λ-return var 0.177 vs S 0.192, MC var 0.342 vs 0.345, Var(V) 0.031 vs 0.066. So G's lower return_var comes from its flatter critic, not from less variable games. Across all four modes in diagnostics' table, the run with the higher EV also has the higher return_var. The part 'G's value function is not much worse' does survive against MC targets: MSE 0.296 vs 0.288 (+3%), EV 0.134 vs 0.166. So the EV gap does overstate the deficit, but '60-75% of the gap comes from G's returns being less variable' is the wrong reason.

I reran synthesis/rr_neff.py: observed residual 1.651; the n_eff=12 transitive null has mean 1.214, 95% range [0.715, 1.839], P = 0.075. This matches the claim. The noise model (per-pair variance from the 512 games / 12) fits greedy pairs having only 12 distinct games, which I confirmed via orbits.py (12 groups of 8, all identical within a group). If anything, n_eff is below 12: some games are decided by start position alone, and 6 complementary pairs is a natural unit. A smaller n_eff only raises p, so the conclusion that intransitivity is not established holds. Modelling the 12 openings as a sample is acknowledged as a choice.

The table numbers come straight from the behaviour outputs, but the framing 'G loses through head-ons' misleads. In constrictor every head-on is mutual by rule (equal lengths, 0 survivors). The G-S head-on itself is symmetric, and G's loss builds up in the 1v1 that follows (G 0.291 in those games; at the first 1v1 moment, 0.406). The colliding G having less room (4.27 vs 6.99) would, if anything, make the trade favourable to G, so it cannot explain the loss. The surviving G has only slightly less room (-0.80). The G-G teammate channel nets only about -0.008 once the S-S games (+0.022) are offset. In sampled play the sign reverses (tailprobe: G 69 vs S 115 teammate collisions). This is descriptive, at one eps level and one seed.

The synthesis labels this speculative, and the supporting evidence is weaker than presented. (a) The value-gradient sharing is mostly in the value head, and in the shared torso constrictor is fairly aligned at 2-3M (see C6). (b) The trap-avoidance and survival lever G shows in royale exists in constrictor, but G has no edge there (see C5). (c) Zero-shot transfer is no better into royale than into constrictor (standard S: 0.098 vs 0.108). (d) An alternative the evidence does not rule out is saturation: constrictor is a short-horizon task. The specialist plateaus near heuristic parity by 3M (0.230, 0.230, 0.234), so there may be little headroom to transfer into. Meanwhile the food-mode specialists sit far below parity (standard 0.028, royale 0.216), leaving room for any extra training signal to help. No ablation tests any of this.

'G told standard 0.225 = told constrictor 0.225' compares a 256-game cell with the 1024-game G,H,H,H cell. On the same 256 game ids, G with the correct label scores 0.245. Paired differences (verify-method/bench_pairs.py): told standard -0.020 [-0.072, +0.033], told duel -0.040 [-0.078, -0.001], told royale -0.024 [-0.070, +0.021]. The duel label's interval excludes 0, and 194-210 of 256 games are identical. So the label is not irrelevant to strength. Since the benchmark gives G the correct label, label confusion still cannot explain the deficit; that part stands. But the test only probes the one-hot. It cannot rule out board-driven cross-mode confusion, which C9 shows exists (G applies moving-tail semantics). 'Established' overstates it.

other_problems: Answer section 2 (royale) cites 'Against heuristics: G-S = +0.176 [+0.140, +0.213]'. That is G minus the 16-minibatch specialist. The correct G minus the 8-minibatch specialist is +0.125 [+0.087, +0.161] (paired bootstrap over the 1024 benchmark game ids, verify-method/bench_pairs.py). The synthesis's row lookup apparently matched 'S16,H,H,H'.

The answer and C9 measure G's deficit against '0.094' (0.5 - 0.406). But 0.406 is the 12 greedy games weighted by how often each config happened to appear in 1024 draws. The protocol's exact value is 5/12, a gap of 0.083, and section 1 itself says that.

Section 1's start-level bootstrap and sign test (from behaviour/extra_constrictor.py) treat 48 placements as independent. They are 6 distinct complementary game pairs, each repeated 8 times. Correct: [0.17, 0.67] over 12 games, p = 0.75; [0.125, 0.71] over 6 pairs, p = 1.0 (verify-method/c1_ci.py).

Diagnostics' 'why G's constrictor returns are less variable is unresolved' is resolved. Logged return_var is the variance of critic-dependent GAE(0.95) returns. Monte Carlo return variance is equal for G and S self-play (0.342 vs 0.345); G's critic is flatter (Var(V) 0.031 vs 0.066). Every EV/return-variance decomposition in diagnostics and the synthesis should be reread with this in mind.

Gradients analysis: 83-99% of the value-term gradient norm lies in the 257-parameter value head (verify-method/vgrad_bias.py). 'Shared value-learning signal' is therefore mostly about the shared linear readout; the torso-level picture at 2-3M is much less separated.
Contradictions item 5 presents G-G teammate collisions as costing G 0.030 share. The S-S collisions in the same table give back +0.022, so the net teammate effect is about -0.008.

The behaviour report's constrictor death-cause labels (self, wall, body) are arbitrary among doomed moves. Diagnostics' and the synthesis's 'self-collision deaths' as a measure of survival learning (C8) carries the same problem into training logs, where deaths per game are fixed at about 3.1 in 4-copy self-play.
All conclusions rest on one training seed per run. Game-level intervals do not cover seed-to-seed variation, which the duel seeds show is large for outcome-type statistics.

Compute used for these checks: about 3 minutes total on core 1 (taskset -c 1). Scripts and outputs are in docs/research/multimode_constrictor_analysis/verify-method/: bench_pairs.py, c1_ci.py, vgrad_bias.py, mc_retvar.py, value_mc.py (output in value_mc_out.txt), flip_margin.py. I also reran behaviour/orbits.py, synthesis/rr_neff.py and synthesis/eps_split.py unchanged. Nothing in the repo was modified.
